column2: Rumaker writes to Olson to confide his terror of the graduation oral before the whole faculty: questioned in a group, his mind panics and goes blank; he asks for a written test and questions Olson about the relation between intuition, feeling, and thought. A reference to his improvised definition of the words “incantation” and “supplication” in class (“a dozen roses,” etc.) and to the word “sensibility,” blurted out without thinking Consequences: Olson will come to see him a few days later to reassure him

A few days after the letter, Olson comes to see Rumaker, reassures him about Shakespeare, and gives him advice on his writing; Rumaker goes back to work on the Shakespeare essays with ardor. Advice: read Shakespeare “as story”; “You need to be modest where you are immodest and immodest where you are modest”; work on the “vectors of force” in his writing Consequences: Rumaker, calmed, goes back to the Shakespeare essays

Olson and Creeley choose Robert Duncan as outside examiner for Rumaker's graduation; Duncan is then living in Majorca with his lover Jess Collins, while the Creeley family stays there and Creeley travels back and forth to teach at Black Mountain. Olson: “We don't want any academic types” Consequences: Duncan will evaluate Rumaker's critical essays and write a glowing report

For their graduation project on the Greeks with Olson (Pausanias, Herodotus, Euripides, Medea, The Trojan Women, the only Greek playwright according to Olson), Dorn and Rumaker drive in the black Morris Minor to the Pack Library in Asheville; after an hour of dusty old books, Dorn drags Rumaker to a blue-collar bar he discovered with Dan Rice, where they drink beer among the mountain people; Rumaker convinces himself that they are doing what Herodotus and Pausanias did: looking and listening out in the world. Dorn's dusty black Morris Minor; Ballantine ale; tall, gaunt customers with angular faces, big eyes and ears, wide-brimmed felt hats pushed back on damp foreheads; the smoke of cheap cigarettes, a dark, yeasty air Consequences: An afternoon of “research” turned into a lesson in living education

One evening in early 1955, after Olson has taken them to the movies in Asheville, the group discusses John Huston's Moby-Dick, then being filmed; Olson, the great Melville specialist, mocks Gregory Peck's “mad coffee-bean eyes” as Ahab and, without having seen anything, is pessimistic because of the problems with the mechanical whale in the Irish Sea and the casting. Peck's eyes called “mad coffee-bean eyes”

Chamberlain, a metal sculptor and former U.S. Navy sailor, who came by way of Chicago and the Art Institute of Chicago, comes to Black Mountain in 1955, persuaded by Jerry Van de Wiele, a former Marine combat artist, who will also persuade Richard Bogart; all three had known one another as students at the Art Institute. Consequences: Chamberlain becomes the only serious sculptor on campus; his work starts to change as soon as he arrives

Elaine, a young, devoutly Catholic artist engaged to John, stays in Chicago to obtain a dispensation from the Vatican allowing her to marry John, who is divorced; John's buddies from Chicago and Detroit rib her for her piety and her refusal to sleep with him before a church wedding; John, frustrated, agrees to wait but eyes the women on campus, especially Connie Olson. Consequences: John without a woman at Black Mountain, like a metal sculptor without a torch

A Sunday softball game: Rumaker pitches wearing an improvised neckerchief, rattling Jorge Fick, who keeps stepping out of the batter's box to protest; Chamberlain umpires and calls a runner safe at first base, covered by Olson; Fee Dawson yells “You motherfucker!”; Olson, seeming to hear the word for the first time, widens his eyes and lets out a thin, high breath, half shock, half delight. Another Sunday, Rumaker, placed in left field, coolly catches a long fly that Bogart, in right field, was already shouting was lost. A roughly laid-out field; handkerchief neckties; smoky poker marathons in an empty study in the Studies Building Consequences: Rumaker tires of the deadly seriousness of the Game and turns it into a “campy” show to defuse the testosterone

The bishop of Raleigh, interested in buying the college as a diocesan retreat, a kind of Black Mountain Notre Dame, tours the grounds with Olson; the Studies Building is swept and cleaned, the windows washed, the broken panes replaced, and Olson asks the remaining students to occupy their studies on Saturday morning, doors open, to look lively; Rumaker is typing when Olson, at his most charming, introduces the bishop, a plump, pasty man in clerical black; Rumaker, disconcerted, nods with a foolish smile. Rumaker's old upright typewriter; a white Roman collar; Olson's remark in class that Christianity became irrelevant when it attacked sex in the 1500s Consequences: Rumaker, at heart resistant to the sale, resigns himself: the end of the school is inevitable

After a night in which Rumaker had to guide Jake, passive, wanting and not wanting, Rumaker begins to resist and then avoid Jake, refusing to use and be used. Whippoorwills singing endlessly in the nearby trees during the night Consequences: Jake feels abandoned, an exclusion that feeds his anger at the party

One afternoon, shortly before the party, Rumaker is reading alone in the kitchen when Jake appears in the doorway, sly, offering his supple swimmer's body, sprawled across from him. Rumaker silently resists, talks about this and that, then looks Jake straight in the eye; Jake looks away, his smile collapses, his eyes take on an icy glaze tinged with fury, and he gets up and leaves without a word. Consequences: A final break between them

The shrinking of the community (a dozen people) has led to the closing of the lower half of the campus; the big dining hall is no longer available or needed for parties, which nonetheless had a long, imaginative tradition at the college. Consequences: Parties are now held in the hall of Streamside
Connie returns from New England with her daughter Kate, perhaps to make one last attempt at patching things up with Charles. Consequences: Her unexpected presence at the party

Jake, legs apart, knees bent, head thrust forward, shoulders hunched, brandishes a beer bottle with a broken neck in a slow, menacing arc, his milky blue eyes turning hard slate, lips curled back to bare his teeth; he threatens everyone. A beer bottle with a shattered neck, cracked glass on the floor Consequences: Joe Fiore steps in

Fiore leaps up from the table, spins Jake around, grabs him by the collar of his T-shirt and the belt of his chinos, yells at him to get out, and gives him a kick so powerful (it lands at the small of his back) that Jake is lifted off the ground; the bottle flies from his fist, and he is propelled outside into the night. Fiore runs to the door to bar his return. T-shirt, chinos, footsteps on the gravel, mountain laurel branches snapping Consequences: Jake flees into the night; Rumaker discovers an unsuspected violence in Fiore
The day after the incident, Jake packs his bags and leaves without a word or a goodbye to anyone. Consequences: Jake's final departure

After the party, too drunk to get back to their rooms (Rumaker lodging at Meadows Inn, Wieners at Streamside itself), they fall asleep in each other's arms, clothed, on bare mattresses pushed into the middle of the hall, without any erotic stirring, seeking warmth and comfort in an animal sleep. A blanket or two, bare mattresses, clothes kept on Consequences: Olson will find them entwined at dawn

Shortly before dawn, in a gray, ashen light, Olson bangs the Dutch door, crosses the hall in one immense stride, the soles of his work shoes passing in an arc over Rumaker's face, followed by another man with a softer step; he flings open every door along the hall, the bathroom included, goes out the back door, down the steps, and across the footbridge over the ravine toward the Studies Building. He finds no one: the next day the whole campus knows that he looked for Connie and Chamberlain in the Studies Building, the Eye, the Stables, and Streamside, in vain. A Dutch door, floors shaking under his steps, Olson's panting breath, a hundred imagined study doors slamming one by one, the wooden footbridge over the ravine Consequences: General rumor; Tom Field thinks Olson would have killed Chamberlain if he had found them together

After the failed party at Streamside, Connie leaves the college again for Massachusetts, with Kate; people take turns keeping Charles company and feeding him. Consequences: Charles isolated, surrounded by friends

Ed Dorn crams Olson, Field, Fick, Wieners, Rumaker, and one or two others into his tiny Morris Minor for an evening of beers prematurely celebrating the coming graduations of Dorn, Fick, and Rumaker. On the way back, merry, Dorn drives past the Gatehouse, takes the back road to the farm, circles and then crosses the cornfield, everyone jolted and laughing over the furrows; Olson enjoys it immensely and shouts to go get Wolpe. Rumaker, loosened by the beer, imitates Wolpe's German accent and his improvised soprano of cries, warbles, and gurgles, which delights Olson. Morris Minor, beers, cornfield furrows Consequences: A rare moment of a relaxed Olson

Coming back from Peak's, Olson, in an expansive mood, spots four or five men fishing illegally at the Lake Eden dam (the lower part of the disused property). He speeds up, brakes sharply, jumps out of the car, and orders them to clear out; the men, including a big, burly, red-faced one in a plaid shirt, refuse. Rumaker, scared to death, pulls at Olson's arm, begging him to let it go. One man says it is plain that he is a Jew and tells him to shut his Jew mouth or they will shut it for him. A fight breaks out (probably provoked by Olson); a punch lands square on Olson's nose and his glasses shatter. Olson, stunned, stares at the broken lenses on the asphalt and repeats that they will have to pay for the repair. Broken lenses on the asphalt, Olson's weak, blurry eyes without glasses, a plaid shirt, Lake Eden, the dam Consequences: Rumaker, terrified, runs for help, then freezes, unable to act

Frightened by the hard violence of these men, like his father's, Rumaker runs for help thinking of Ed Dorn, then stops dead in the middle of the wooded path, halfway between the dining hall and the scene of the fight, unable to go forward or back. A wooded path; the memory of a fifth-grade fight in which he had broken a tooth of Joey Haley's Consequences: A sense of having betrayed Olson

That evening, Tom Field, an excellent cook, has prepared a special meal: Olson's first dinner at their place, the three of them in the big front room with the enormous fireplace. Olson, without his usual appetite, says little, except that in America one never gets the chance to know what kind of man one is. Rumaker, with no appetite, feels Olson's eyes on him signifying his betrayal; Tom chatters cheerfully, as he does when he entertains. Rumaker drinks heavily without getting drunk. A big fireplace, a meal cooked by Field Consequences: A lasting wound between Rumaker and Olson

Creeley's teaching deteriorates: his students often have to extract him physically from Ma Peak's (usually Cynthia Homire) to bring him back in time for his evening class in the Reading Room. Consequences: His teaching declines

One evening, brought back once again by Cynthia Homire, Creeley, acid and stiff on his chair under the windows, goes around the class pouring out on each student a vicious, threatening assessment of his or her failings as a human being and incurable worthlessness as a writer; to Rumaker he sneers, asking what's wrong with him, does he bathe too much? A chair under the windows of the Reading Room Consequences: A wound for Rumaker, who recognizes a grain of truth
Olson, Rumaker's adviser, sets up with him for his graduation project work on Shakespeare and the Greeks. Consequences: Added pressure in an already overloaded summer.

Rumaker worries about the 1955 recession and the scarcity of jobs, about his ability to “pass” (to hide the Black Mountain rebel and the homosexuality), and about the draft: with his 2-S deferment, would he declare himself homosexual at induction to become 4-F, and with what stigma when looking for work? The Pentagon was in fact cracking down on malingerers; Ed Dorn had himself feigned homosexuality to escape service. 2-S deferment, the dreaded 4-F status. Consequences: Drained energies, nervous wear.

Earlier in the spring of 1955, a troubled, effeminate young man from the South, claiming to be related to Tennessee Williams and come to study acting, had taken an overdose of pills in his room upstairs at Streamside and had to be rushed to the hospital in Asheville to have his stomach pumped.

Right after his graduation ceremony, Rumaker takes down from the shelf above his study door three piles of manuscripts a foot high, written before and during Black Mountain, and burns them in an old rusty oil drum used as a trash can in front of the Stables (the painters' studios). Three piles a foot high; a rusty drum; sparks rising into the night sky Consequences: He feels unburdened, light; he packs his bags that very night and leaves in the morning, hitchhiking north for the last time

Walking back down to Meadows Inn in the dark (after three years he knows every stone and root on the path), he stops on the wooden bridge to listen one last time to the invisible stream in the ravine. He moves in temporarily with friends in a tiny Father-Son-Holy Ghost house, former eighteenth-century servants' quarters: three small rooms stacked one above the other. A wooden bridge; the stream in the ravine; three stacked rooms on an alley Consequences: A new start

Around the mid-1950s, Bill's canvases sell for several thousand dollars apiece; the year-end totals exceed anything the couple had known; he can at last afford the quality paints, brushes, and canvases he used to buy by sacrificing rent or meals.

Joan and her twin sister Nancy, who had come to study art, lived in an apartment paid for by their father on East Eighth Street, around the corner from the Cedar; Nancy went out with Franz Kline, Joan with Bill, whose serious interest frightened Elaine. Consequences: Joan's pregnancy will follow; Elaine felt her marriage threatened

When Joan became pregnant by him, Bill showed obvious joy, at the Cedar as well as in Elaine's eyes, and told friends that he was expecting “dis baby.” The phrase “dis baby” (this baby, in his accent) Consequences: Elaine's depression and drinking bouts

Albers writes to President Griswold to denounce the disparity, apparently peculiar to Street Hall, between work done and pay: the young who have given everything do not have the security of the old who hardly work anymore; he asks for more equal treatment. A tenured professor with no students in the department remains paid out of the salary budget Consequences: His appeals have no effect
He travels on the French Line, lands at Le Havre, and goes on to Ulm via Paris, which he had not seen since 1929. The French Line; last visit to Paris in 1929.

Delighted with his spacious quarters in the new buildings, Albers is pampered by the housekeeper Frau Hausele, an alert, sparkling mama who keeps everything in order and absolutely correct; she does his laundry, polishes his shoes, mends his clothes; he calls her a Swabian pearl and the kind of person who restores one's faith in humanity. Laundry, polished shoes, mended clothes.

After the temporary premises downtown since 1953, the move into the new facilities enormously improves working conditions; he writes to Anni that everything seems about to begin, teaching included: they are waiting for him to get things started. Very spacious buildings, many workshops and offices, staircases on every side. Consequences: The school's real beginning.

The Dutch Constructivist is not his cup of tea, he writes to Anni; to avoid the opening of his exhibition at the local museum, he goes off on a weekend excursion to Stuttgart, where he is glad to see Tut Schlemmer and her family again. The opening avoided; a weekend in Stuttgart.

Albers writes to Anni that they drove to Zurich in Bill's Bentley (with a Rolls-Royce engine) to see the big traveling Mondrian exhibition at the Kunsthaus. A Bentley with a Rolls-Royce engine; all of Bill's suits in cashmere

The Yale Corporation dissolves the Division of the Arts, creates a separate Department of Drama, and makes the art gallery autonomous; the school becomes the Department of Architecture and Design; the new committee is chaired by Robert Osborn.

Invited by Schweikher, Anni gives one spring a series of early-morning seminars to a few architecture students: textiles as the first architectural “ceiling,” learning to weave with cards; McNair still keeps his cards. Early-morning seminars; black and white threads producing a textile band about an inch wide; the drafting room on the top floor

Taking advantage of Sawyer's absence in Europe, Schweikher calms the storm by sacrificing Nalle; he writes to Sawyer to justify himself, citing the faculty's extreme pressure and asking Albers to contact Rudolph Schwartz through Max Bill. Letter quoted: the faculty's pressure to get rid of Nalle was extreme; keeping Nalle was his own stubbornness Consequences: Nalle's contract terminated in early 1956

During three weeks of teaching at Haystack, Anni writes to Josef in Ulm a series of quick notes about the rumor of Sawyer's departure, then plays it down, then worries about it again; Josef replies curtly. Notes written before breakfast, two days and then three days apart; the rumor comes from Mr. Merritt Consequences: The rumor will prove partly accurate
Schnaidt studies with Albers at Ulm in the summer of 1955; he writes to the author on November 22, 2004 (in French).

Four works shown: two glass pictures, City (1928) and Windows (1929), and two Homages to the Square, Apodictic (1950-54) and Mittelwort (1954) City at the Kunsthaus Zurich; Windows at the Westfälisches Landesmuseum in Münster

The Austrian student, already the author of a series of architectural screen walls, arrives at RISD on a Fulbright scholarship; the following year, at Albers's invitation, he becomes a postgraduate at Yale and pursues his continuous modular structures based on the saddle shape.
In a letter supporting her application to the Guggenheim Foundation, Fuller praises Larsen's photographic vision.
The first polio vaccine becomes available, ending the national anxiety about the body in the 1950s
Asawa's interest in large pieces ends her brief collaboration with the Peridot Gallery in New York, whose eight-foot ceiling limits the exploration of large sculptures. An 8-foot ceiling

The New York gallery's eight-foot ceiling limited large pieces; Asawa's interest in large-scale experiment helped end the collaboration. In 1955, sculptures thirteen feet tall and forty-two inches in diameter; full-size drawings to design the forms. Consequences: Asawa turns toward architecture and design.

The dialogue with interior design leads Asawa to apply for a Guggenheim fellowship for sculptures for architectural use in large indoor or outdoor spaces. Technical challenges cited: preventing rust, tarnish, and discoloration.
A sculpture by Asawa is shown at the 1955 São Paulo Bienal. Consequences: A possible link with the Brazilian Neo-Concrete context (Max Bill, Lygia Clark).

A stained-glass window of thirty-one panels of Corning photosensitive glass set in an existing wooden frame, entirely in shades of gray, without traditional leading, thanks to the chemical treatment of glass that reacts to light. 31 panels; photosensitive glass; a single material exploited to the full Consequences: Links the work to the Bauhaus “wall glass paintings”
Designs the costumes for two performances by Taylor and for Circus Polka.
In 1955 Rauschenberg moves to a studio on Pearl Street, where he develops the Combine paintings. Consequences: The birth and rise of the Combine painting on Pearl Street

A quilt, sheet, and pillow fastened to a stretcher: the upper half linen painted gesturally (clots, drips, directional brushstrokes), the lower half a patterned quilt left almost untouched except for a few splashes. The dented pillow (more so originally than today) and the turned-down sheet suggest a recent departure. A dented pillow (more so originally than today), a turned-down sheet
The black and red paintings were made in a studio on Fulton Street; in 1955 he moves to Pearl Street, where the combine paintings develop. Consequences: The birth of the combine painting format.

In the spring of 1955, lacking canvas, Rauschenberg uses his own pillow, sheet, and patchwork quilt to make Bed. Pillow, sheet, the patchwork quilt from his bed Consequences: A founding work of the “combine,” a term he coins in 1955

A major Combine: a canvas covered with a paisley shawl forming an active decorative ground; a Wanted poster and its catalog of criminal traits, an arrow toward a fallen figure, a striped book cover, a fragment of the Manhattan telephone directory: themes of the delinquent and of urban downward mobility, with no clear narrative message, leaving the deciphering to the viewer. Paisley shawl, Wanted poster, fragment of the Manhattan directory Consequences: The consecration of openness to the viewer as a guiding aesthetic element

In the spring, Rauschenberg shows his combines in the “Fourth Annual Exhibition of Painting and Sculpture”; Short Circuit incorporates paintings by Weil and Johns and a collage by Ray Johnson, artists absent from the exhibition A collaboration with three artists

After the outcry from conservative critics that followed the award of the Prix des Critiques to The Voyeur, Robbe-Grillet receives warm support from Breton; he will later admit to having had Surrealist tendencies at certain moments. The Prix des Critiques awarded to The Voyeur (1955). Consequences: Shows that the Nouveau Roman is not categorically rejected by Breton, despite the refusal of metaphor proclaimed by Robbe-Grillet in “Nature, humanisme, tragédie” (1958).

Despite the outcry from conservative critics after the award of the Prix des Critiques to The Voyeur, Robbe-Grillet receives warm encouragement from Breton; he will later admit to having harbored Surrealist tendencies at certain moments. Consequences: The Nouveau Roman is not categorically rejected by Breton (statement to the Nouvel Observateur in 1964).

Bataille argues that the meaning of the painting Olympia (1863) lies not in the text behind it but in its obliteration; Manet reduced what he saw to the simple, mute fullness of what was there, against Valéry's metaphorical reading (a metaphor of woman, of urban prostitution). Olympia, 1863 Consequences: This asymbolic reading foreshadows Barthes's reading of Rauschenberg and Pop

Lebel has his first solo show, in Florence; the oil on panel Iceberg de poche: Portrait of Diana, dedicated to Breton, is given to him the following year. His first Paris show takes place in 1957 at the Galerie Iris Clert, before Rauschenberg's telegram for Iris Clert's exhibition of portraits (1961).

They discuss a system of secondary schools (and a few colleges) of arts and sciences in the manner of Black Mountain: composition, performance, and exhibition as basic factors, a school in every neighborhood, in any country. An emphasis on the arts; the idea that art, according to Stephen Spender, is the conquest of self-consciousness Consequences: A project that remained an idea

Unable to interpret a dream he had around 1950, and with the school going to ruin at the end of 1955, Olson withdraws to his house to work entirely on the Maximus Letters. Consequences: Heralds the end of the college; the campus becomes deserted and disorderly

In an essay, Cage writes that the word “experimental” is apt if it describes not an act to be judged afterward as a success or failure, but an act whose outcome is unknown. A quotation from the 1955 essay Consequences: A break with Albers's definition of the test

Asked by John McHale of the London Independent Group about the Bauhaus's influence, Fuller answers curtly that there is none, singling out two major methodological differences: technological teleology as an absolute principle, and the importance of how structures are built and work, as against aesthetic appearance. Consequences: A public assertion of his break with the Bauhaus legacy.

A paperback collection of several of Rice's stories, with a preface by Erskine Caldwell praising his understanding of Southern Black and white people and the way they read each other's unspoken thoughts and unrevealed acts.
Nell Rice leaves Black Mountain and joins her ailing brother in Princeton, New Jersey.
Begins the series of abstract urban landscapes and merges the woman and landscape motifs; separates from Elaine.

Joanne Schieble, pregnant by Jandali, a Syrian Muslim teaching assistant, takes refuge with a San Francisco doctor who delivers the child and arranges the adoption. Her dying father, a mink farmer near Green Bay, had threatened to disinherit her. The child is adopted by Paul and Clara Jobs, married for nine years and childless after an ectopic pregnancy. Summer 1954 spent in Syria; mink farm; Clara's ectopic pregnancy; adoption nine years after the marriage Consequences: Jobs will never bear the names of his biological parents

Back from Rome, Ben is quietly jubilant at his recognition, but the tension mounts. One night Rumaker gives in to Ben out of gratitude; afterward he turns away when Ben seeks him, with a twinge of empathy, remembering Merrill's cold shoulders at Black Mountain. One morning when he happens to surprise Ben masturbating in the bathroom, Ben, furious, yells at him to clear out. Ben nonetheless helps him find jobs so he can move out. “I want you out of here!” Consequences: Leaving the apartment; the search for a job and a room.

Ben suggests a part-time job: reading to a wealthy old woman who is losing her sight, a friend of Carson McCullers, who had come to visit her a week earlier, paralyzed down her left side after a stroke. A buttoned-up young man, the lady's protégé, obviously gay, comes to size Rumaker up; his cold, appraising look makes Rumaker understand that he will not get the job he desperately needs. The old lady's remark: “so young and so lame all down her left side”. Consequences: Failure; Rumaker keeps looking.

After making the rounds of the agencies (where an interviewer warns him not to say he lives in Greenwich Village, with its sinful reputation), Rumaker, his hair shaggy, a product of the “commie-homo” Black Mountain, is hired as a clerk-typist at IBM World Trade, the most ultraconservative outfit there is. A salary of $60 a week, $12 more than at Prentice-Hall the winter before. He lies to the personnel department, promising a lifelong career at IBM, while he plans to head back to the Swannanoa valley in early March. Six temporary weeks with the possibility of a permanent job. $60 a week; $12 more than at Prentice-Hall; six weeks announced. Consequences: Savings possible to return to Black Mountain at the end of March.

Woody, contacted as soon as he arrived in New York, gives him two of his expensive tweed suits, one blue, one brown, still in good condition though out of mothballs since the 1930s, plus two button-down shirts from the '30s still in their original Macy's wrapping, never worn; Woody apparently throws nothing away despite his small apartment. At IBM, where a dark suit and tie are de rigueur, no one comments on Rumaker's anachronistic, mothball-smelling getup, or on his long, ragged hair as against the preferred “butch cut.” Consequences: Rumaker can work without remarks.

Alan Watson, the founder's younger son, in charge of IBM World Trade, often appears unannounced, prowling as if on a dangerous mission; he catches sight of Rumaker over the wall of filing cabinets that isolates the small department at the back, stares at his clothes and hair (Rumaker is waiting for his first paycheck to get a haircut), and asks Connolly sotto voce who he is. Rumaker, heart pounding, fears being unmasked as a student from the commie/homo Black Mountain, a liar and a mocker (he has compared IBM computers to coffins of the dead, over a forbidden lunch of Dubonnet at Ferdi's with Marisa Traina, another secret mocker). Watson nods briefly and moves on. Dubonnet cocktails at Ferdi's; computers “exactly like the grimmest caskets of the dead”; the UNIVAC shown by Glenn Lewis at Princeton a few years earlier. Consequences: Rumaker keeps his job.

A room comes free upstairs at the top of the long, wide staircase; Ben arranges with the superintendent and his wife (an old, graying couple whom Ben describes as given to the cheap liquor made in their basement) for Rumaker to move into the same house as he. At the top of a long, wide staircase; liquor fermented in the basement. Consequences: Rumaker has a roof of his own.

Shortly after landing the IBM job, Rumaker gets an upstairs room at the top of a wide staircase, which Ben has negotiated with the superintendent and his wife. He savors his privacy, far from Ben's sharp tongue. $7 a week; a room the size of a telephone booth; a narrow camp bed wedged against a small cigarette-burned table; an alcove closet hidden by a drab curtain; a high ceiling; a six-over-six window looking out on the gardens of St. John's; a shared bathroom in the hall; owner: the church of St. John's-in-the-Village; boozy superintendents distilling their liquor in the basement Consequences: Independence from Ben, a space to write

Rumaker takes Jack, a Dutch journalist and budding novelist, to a revival of Camille with Greta Garbo. Sitting in the nearly empty back row, a winter coat over their knees, Jack squeezes his hand under the coat throughout the film, until the bones of his fingers hurt, before Greta's death, not a hair out of place. A nearly empty theater, the back row, a heavy winter coat shared over their knees Consequences: Rumaker both attracted and frightened by Jack's strength

One Saturday afternoon, Jack says he just happened to be passing through the neighborhood; Rumaker later suspects an arranged meeting, Jack having wheedled out his address. Rumaker reads in his eyes the invitation to go up to his room (Jack shares an apartment uptown with two Dutchmen who know nothing of his private life); intimidated, he flees on the pretext of a pressing appointment and feels relief as he walks down Christopher Street. Saturday afternoon; Jack's perfect English, slightly Dutch-accented Consequences: Jack's barely perceptible disappointment, too proud to admit a refusal

Rumaker's only sexual adventure in his room: after a night of bars, both tipsy, they throw the mattress on the floor to make room; the room is cramped and the walls thin. The mattress thrown on the floor

In January, in his claustrophobic closet, Rumaker is possessed by a story that consumes all his waking hours and his dreams for weeks: notes stolen at the IBM office in a pocket notebook, then typed on the sly on his IBM electric typewriter; evenings and weekends, shut in his room, draft after draft by hand. Unable to buy or rent a typewriter, and refusing to borrow Ben's, he borrows Merrill's old Remington portable from his loft on Rivington Street. The final title “The Pipe,” preferred to “Mud.” A pocket notebook; an IBM electric typewriter; Merrill's Remington portable; the abandoned title “Mud” Consequences: The story possesses him for several years; it was never finished with him

On a bitterly cold night, after work, Rumaker takes the subway to Merrill's former-factory loft (Herb having stayed in Houston): grimy bricks painted white, plastic nailed over the broken windows and bellying in the wind, a Japanese lamp with a rice-paper shade bought at a high price. Rumaker unrolls the manuscript from his pocket and reads, stumbling, the steam of his breath coming out of his mouth; Merrill listens with an attentive, quietly amused smile; he liked being read to, as in their evenings at Black Mountain. A former factory loft; a Japanese rice-paper globe lamp, fashionable among BMC expatriates “into Zen,” customers of the Orientalia Bookstore Consequences: The first listener to the story read aloud

Rumaker talks about his story to Marisa Traina, a beautiful transplant from San Francisco who also aspires to write, with whom he drinks Dubonnet cocktails at lunchtime at Ferdi's despite the ban (time cards stamped in red ink for lateness, the boss John Connolly seeing everything but saying nothing). Marisa reads the story and hands it back: it's not exactly Not as a Stranger. A practicing Catholic secretary, newly married, who reminds him of his sister Mary, insists on reading it: cheeks flushed, pale blue eyes confused, she says she has never read anything like it and is very impressed. Dubonnet cocktails at Ferdi's; a time card in red ink; a reference to Morton Thompson's best-selling novel Consequences: In retrospect Rumaker sees it as a test to decide whether he would show the story to his sister and his mother

The student Maurice Goldring writes to Albers that the second Grundkurs emphasizes the mathematical demonstration of ideas, leaving little to experiment with firsthand; under the influence of Max Bill and the Argentine concretist Tomás Maldonado, the school is sliding toward the accepted language of Swiss and South American concrete art; several students await with relief the return of Albers, a rare teacher able to communicate his enthusiasm and insisting that the student make his own experience rather than copy. Consequences: Anticipation of Albers's return in the summer of 1955.

Leaves Fulton Street for a new studio; Johns has a studio in the same building and becomes a close friend; together they decorate windows for Tiffany and Bonwit Teller, then get other freelance contracts through the agent Emile de Antonio. Department store windows Consequences: Financing for their artistic work
Médium: Communication surréaliste no. 4 publishes the expulsion (“A son gré”) of Max Ernst. Médium no. 4, January 1955, p. 36 Consequences: The context of the internal vendetta within Surrealism

The baseball player asks to see the sports paintings, looks without being disconcerted, and says “I'll take these six”, a record purchase for Elaine. Words: “I'll take these six”; “I just liked his style”. Atmosphere: A joyful meeting of two worlds.

The six students run from class to class, changing disguises every few minutes, to make the inspectors believe in a flourishing community Atmosphere: The tragic farce of the college's end Stakes: Desperate economic survival, dignity sacrificed

For several days, they wander the fields, looking up, listening for the sound of the rich Southerner's private plane, which was to tip its wings to promise a bequest Atmosphere: An empty sky, an absurd and pathetic wait Stakes: The last financial hope of the dying college

A man arrives at night and climbs the mountain by the glow of a few lamps; he finds two people drinking coffee who encourage him: others are around, and he will meet them in the morning; the man, nervous at the ghost-town atmosphere, calls a taxi and leaves at dawn. Words: The two residents, cheerfully: other people are around, and he will meet them tomorrow Atmosphere: Night, sparse lights, coffee, an unsettling silence Stakes: The contrast between the quiet hospitality of the last residents and the image of ruin seen from outside.

An exchange of letters: Olson argues for the dual responsibility; Forbes, shocked by the crazy tone of the appeals and by Nell Rice's tales, refuses, grants two postponements (April 1954, April 1955), then sets the ultimatum of June 29; Mary Fiore brings the $5,250; Huss coldly notifies him of the deposit in escrow; Forbes returns the documents with a bitter note of farewell. Words: Forbes: “I am sorry my association with Black Mountain College should end in this fashion, but I am glad it is ending, for I simply do not have the faith in Charles Olson that I have had in previous Rectors”; Olson: “The College . . . matters to the society” Atmosphere: Notarial solemnity, contained rancor Stakes: The very existence of the college is at stake in an exchange of letters.

Betty as Desdemona on the mattress laid on the gray floor; Rumaker as Othello lightly lays the pillow over her face; seized by the feeling of murder, he trembles, tears away the pillow, and stops the scene; Betty sits up, smiling and puzzled; Wes has understood and gotten what he wanted Words: Othello's lines: 'Put out the light, and then put out the light…' Atmosphere: Morning, gray concrete, tension between acting and reality, the vertigo of a simulated murder Stakes: The actor discovers that acting can go beyond acting

Betty, as the mother, announces the hereditary syphilis; Rumaker as Oswald stares at the stream through the window and stands silent long after the scene is over, his mind empty; turning around, he finds Betty and Wes looking at him, Wes with moist eyes Words: Wes to Betty: imagine his brain turning to mush Atmosphere: A noisy stream, a prolonged silence, the accidental grace of Zen emptiness Stakes: The right effect achieved without seeking the effect; the only time Rumaker sees Wes moved

Rumaker is reading in bed; a heavy step on the outside stairs, a soft knock, Betty's voice and then Olson's, the bedsprings starting to twang for nearly half an hour under Charles's weight; Rumaker imagines the bed crashing through the ceiling and the headlines in the Asheville Citizen, and compares Betty to a single rosebud bearing the whole bush Words: Imagined headlines: 'STUDENT KILLED BY AMOROUS TEACHER', 'VICTIM CRUSHED BY FALLING LOVENEST' Atmosphere: Darkness, wide-open eyes, a mixture of comedy, Oedipal anguish, and a sense of betrayal on Connie's behalf Stakes: The fall of the spiritual father; Rumaker hears his god with feet of clay and relives his childhood in New Jersey

The manuscripts all come back rejected; Rumaker shows Olson the single word in pencil at the top of his copy; Olson gives him a broad smile. Words: the word “Ugh”; Olson's smile says they know better than these judges Atmosphere: A painful disappointment turned into initiation, a loss of innocence Stakes: Rumaker's first confrontation with the outside world after the praise of the class

Wieners reads his snobbishly academic critique of “The Pipe” (fake Southern Faulkner, etc.); Olson attacks him vehemently for his misreadings and orders him to learn to read; Wieners, disconcerted but admiring, surrenders. Words: Olson: he has it all wrong; he has to learn to read Atmosphere: A baptism of fire, pedagogical violence, conversion Stakes: Olson captures a new disciple for his enchanted circle

On a shortcut, they find an overturned red convertible, the bloody driver lying on the road; Tom, a former medic, slaps his cheeks to revive him and sends a motorist to find a telephone; John, terrified, murmurs that the blond looks like Dana; sirens, state police, an ambulance takes the pallid injured man to Asheville; on the way back, Tom chatters cheerfully while boiling coffee on the Coleman until Rumaker wants to hit him; that night John writes a poem about the accident, with Dana woven into it. Words: John: the injured man looks like Dana; Tom: he saw worse in Korea Atmosphere: Headlights sweeping the red clay ditch, country music on the convertible's radio, smoke and steam under the chassis, mute horror Stakes: An omen: Rumaker will later see it as the first sign of the end of Black Mountain

Wieners chatters, hands flying; on the other side, players in dirty uniforms whisper and laugh, looking at their table. Egged on by his buddies, the blond crosses the room with a stiff, uncertain step, a dead cigarette at the corner of his mouth. He leans on the table, gripping its edge with his fingers. Rumaker, heart hammering, takes the matches from his pack of Home Runs and strikes one; the young man cups his hands around Rumaker's, trembling so hard he makes Rumaker's hands shake. Cigarette lit, he mumbles “'Bliged,” nods, and quickly leaves. His teammates slap him on the back and the rear as after a home run; he sits back down, relieved and delighted. Words: “Uh — y'all got a light?” in a tense voice, staring at Rumaker; then a barely audible “'Bliged” Atmosphere: The sweat and dust of the game, suspicious tension, both pairs of hands trembling, final relief Stakes: The valley's latent homophobia brushes against violence; desire and fear overlap in a single gesture
